Bug_Details:
Reference equality used to compare arrays Generally when comparing arrays for equality, the programmer intends to check
that the contents of the arrays are equal rather than that they are actually the
same object. But many commonly used equals methods compare arrays for reference
equality rather than content equality. These include the instance .equals()
method, Guava’s com.google.common.base.Objects#equal(), JDK’s
java.util.Objects#equals(), and Android’s
androidx.core.ObjectsCompat#equals(). If reference equality is needed, == should be used instead for clarity.
Otherwise, use java.util.Arrays#equals() to compare the contents of the
arrays.
Bug_Explanation: The bug was embedded in the generated code by using the.equals() method on arrays, which checks for reference equality rather than content equality. This is incorrect for comparing the contents of two integer arrays.
Trigger_Explanation: The generated JUnit test cases call the showBug method of the ArrayEqualityBug class, which uses the.equals() method on arrays to compare them. Since.equals() checks for reference equality, the tests will fail when the arrays have the same contents but different references, and pass only when the arrays are the exact same object in memory.
Bug_Trigger_Explanation: The test results indicate that all three tests passed, which means the method'showBug' returned false for cases where the arrays have the same contents but different references (testShowBugWithSameContentsDifferentReferences), different contents (testShowBugWithDifferentContents), and the same reference (testShowBugWithSameReference). This confirms that the bug is triggered because the method incorrectly uses reference equality instead of content equality.
